screens.title: Presence, Typing Indicators, and Read Receipts
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how presence, typing indicators, and read receipts turn a basic messaging pipeline into a responsive, social experience. Presence tells the system who is available now; typing indicators give real-time micro-feedback that someone intends to send a message; and read receipts close the loop so senders know their message was actually seen. These features are small at the UI level but require careful architecture at scale. We will use Redis for fast presence storage and Pub/Sub for ephemeral events, discuss heartbeats that prevent stale online statuses, and examine how message state moves from sent to delivered to read. You will also see practical trade-offs: how frequent heartbeats affect load, why typing events must be debounced, and how read receipts introduce write amplification and privacy decisions. By the end you should be able to design a dedicated Presence Service, implement typing broadcasts for small conversations, and choose an approach for read receipts that balances accuracy, performance, and user privacy. Consider: when would you accept eventual consistency for read receipts versus needing near-real-time certainty?

screens.title: Presence Service: responsibilities and data model
screens.narratorSegment: A Presence Service has three core responsibilities: record when a user connects or disconnects, expose a way to query a user's status, and notify interested parties when statuses change. Practically, that means storing a small record per user—status, last_seen timestamp, and the server_id that hosts the connection. Redis is an excellent fit because it is in-memory, fast, and offers atomic hash operations for these small records. A common key design is presence:user_id mapped to a hash with fields status, last_seen, and server_id. This keeps reads and writes O(1) and keeps the data model simple for other services to consume. The service should expose two access patterns: direct lookups for on-demand queries, and Pub/Sub notifications for real-time subscribers. One important misconception to avoid is believing a single central store is enough for availability; use clustering or sharding to distribute load. Also avoid storing large session blobs in presence records—keep the data minimal to prevent excessive memory pressure. A correct design isolates presence as a small, horizontally scalable microservice that answers the binary but time-sensitive question: is this user online right now?

Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Presence Service
Core Concept

Presence responsibilities

Record connects/disconnects, support queries, and broadcast status changes to subscribers.

Presence record (example)
Key: presence:user_id — Fields: status, last_seen, server_id
Keep records minimal to reduce memory use and to make notifications fast.
Queries
Read presence:user_id for instant status checks.
Notifications
Publish change events to channels so subscribing services can react in real time.
Architecture view
Why Redis?
  • In-memory speed for frequent reads and writes.
  • Atomic hash updates for simple state records.
  • Built-in Pub/Sub for ephemeral notifications.
Common misconception:
Don’t use Redis as your single durable store for long session history. Presence data is ephemeral; keep the footprint small and rely on clustering for availability.
Key Takeaway

Treat presence as a minimal, in-memory service: fast reads, atomic updates, and Pub/Sub notifications for real-time UX.

screens.title: Storing presence in Redis
screens.narratorSegment: When you store presence in Redis, pick a compact, consistent key pattern and keep the record tiny. A common pattern is presence:user_id mapped to a Redis hash with fields status, last_seen, and server_id. Status is a short string like online or offline; last_seen is a timestamp used to detect stale heartbeats; server_id indicates which chat server currently hosts that connection. Hashes are ideal because they allow atomic updates to individual fields without replacing the entire value. Avoid storing session-heavy data or long JSON blobs in presence keys. Instead, store only the information needed for other services to decide whether to push a notification or to display an online badge. Also consider TTLs for inactive keys so memory clears for long-away users. Remember a misconception: Redis persistence options exist, but presence usually relies on in-memory semantics and Pub/Sub; don't rely on persistence for presence correctness. Instead, use clustering and replication to handle availability and failover. Storing presence in Redis means use presence:user_id → hset fields status, last_seen, server_id and ttl to evict stale entries.. In practical terms, key patterns: hashes, keys, and what to store. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Storing presence in Redis
Definition

Key design: presence:user_id

Store just status, last_seen, and server_id in a hash for atomic updates and small memory footprint.

Example fields
  • status: "online" or "offline"
  • last_seen: epoch timestamp
  • server_id: which chat_server holds the connection
Use short TTLs or eviction policies for truly inactive accounts to recover memory.
Practical notes
  • Hashes allow updating last_seen without rewriting the whole record.
  • Keep values small to reduce replication and memory pressure.
  • Do not persist presence to the message DB; it is ephemeral by nature.
Pitfall
Avoid treating Redis presence keys as durable audit logs. They can be evicted and are not designed for long-term storage.
Key Takeaway

Reserve Redis hashes for minimal, high-speed presence records; keep them small and ephemeral.

screens.title: Heartbeats and timeout detection
screens.narratorSegment: Heartbeats are periodic keep-alive signals that tell the Presence Service a client is still connected. A typical pattern is for a chat server to send a heartbeat for each connected client every fixed interval, for example every five seconds. The Presence Service updates last_seen when it receives a heartbeat. If last_seen is older than an offline timeout window—commonly 30 to 60 seconds—the Presence Service marks the user offline. This handles abrupt network drops where the server does not receive a formal disconnect. Implementing heartbeats requires careful tuning: a very short interval increases load and network chatter, while a very long interval delays detection of offline clients. Another important point is to avoid relying solely on TCP disconnect events; those are not always delivered promptly. Use heartbeats plus graceful disconnects when possible. A common misconception is that a single missed heartbeat should immediately make a user offline; instead, use a timeout window to avoid flapping for temporary network jitter. In short, heartbeats provide liveness information that the Presence Service uses to keep online state accurate. Heartbeats and timeout detection means send regular heartbeats and mark offline after a timeout window; tune interval versus timeout to balance accuracy and load.. In practical terms, how chat servers keep presence accurate when clients disconnect abruptly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Heartbeats
Process Flow

Heartbeat lifecycle

  1. Client connects to Chat Server; server marks user online.
  2. Chat Server sends periodic heartbeats to Presence Service updating last_seen.
  3. If heartbeats stop and last_seen exceeds timeout, Presence Service marks user offline.
Tune heartbeat interval and offline timeout to avoid false offline states while keeping detection prompt.
Practical considerations
  • Debounce server-side events to avoid flapping.
  • Use a slightly longer timeout than the heartbeat interval to allow for brief jitter.
  • Combine graceful disconnect messages with heartbeats for fast and correct offline marking.
Misconception
Do not mark offline on a single missed heartbeat; rely on the timeout window to reduce incorrect offline markings during transient network issues.
Key Takeaway

Heartbeats plus a sensible timeout are the reliable method to detect abrupt disconnects without frequent false positives.

screens.title: Typing indicators: events and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Typing indicators are small ephemeral events that make conversations feel active. The canonical flow is simple: when a user begins typing the client sends a typing_start event to its Chat Server; the server publishes the event to a Pub/Sub channel for that chat_id; other clients subscribed to that chat receive the event and display "User X is typing...". When typing stops—either after a timeout on inactivity or when the message is sent—the client sends typing_stop and the event is broadcast. In practice there are several important best practices. First, debounce typing_start on the client so you don’t publish an event on every keypress. A common pattern is to send typing_start once and then suppress further events for a short window. Second, restrict typing indicators to direct messages or small group chats; in large public channels typing indicators create noise. Third, treat typing events as ephemeral: do not persist them to the message database. Redis Pub/Sub is ideal for this ephemeral broadcast because it keeps the pipeline simple without creating durable writes. Be aware of network load and avoid sending high-frequency typing updates from low-quality connections. Finally, remember that indicators are UI affordances — they do not guarantee a message will be sent.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Typing Indicators
Process Flow

Typing start → broadcast → typing stop

Clients emit typing_start, servers publish to chat:chat_id, subscribers display ephemeral indicator, and typing_stop ends the indicator.
Best practices
  • Debounce client events to avoid spamming Pub/Sub channels.
  • Limit scope to DMs and small groups.
  • Do not persist typing events to the message store.
Common mistakes
  • Sending updates on every keystroke without debounce.
  • Broadcasting typing indicators in very large channels.
  • Treating typing indicators as durable; they should be ephemeral.
Pro tip

Debounce on the client for 300–1000ms and send a single typing_start, then send typing_stop after a short idle window or on message send.

screens.title: Read receipts: sent, delivered, read
screens.narratorSegment: Read receipts describe stages of a message lifecycle that inform the sender about delivery and consumption. Start with a sent state when the message is persisted to the message store and acknowledged by the sender's client. A delivered state is reached when the message is successfully pushed to the recipient's client and the client acknowledges receipt with an ACK. A read state occurs when the recipient actually views the message, for example when the message is scrolled into view or when the conversation becomes active; the client sends a read event for that message_id or the last message seen. To support these states you need a status field in the messages table, and ideally a mechanism to update that field when ACK or read events arrive. In group chats, tracking per-user read for every message is write-heavy; common strategies are to maintain a last_read pointer per user per conversation or to provide a read-by count. Privacy is important: users should be able to disable read receipts, which changes how and whether the client sends read events. The correct model maps UI expectations to minimal database writes while preserving reasonable accuracy for sender feedback.

keyIdea.title: Message lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Track sent when persisted, delivered on client ACK, and read when client signals viewing; model per-user or last-read strategies for groups.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Read Receipts
Definition

Sent → Delivered → Read

Sent
Message persisted and sender confirmed save.
Delivered
Recipient device received the message; client sent ACK.
Read
Recipient viewed the message; client emitted read for message_id or last seen.
For group chats, consider tracking last_read per user or a read-by count instead of storing per-message per-user read flags to reduce write amplification.
Common misconception

Assuming delivered implies read. Delivery only means device received the message; reading requires an explicit user action or UI visibility event.

screens.title: Strategies for read receipts in group chats
screens.narratorSegment: Group chats present a scaling problem for read receipts. One approach is to record a read flag for every message and every member, which gives precise per-user per-message visibility but generates a huge number of writes as each user reads messages. An alternative is to maintain a last_read pointer per user per conversation: when a user reads up to message X, update their last_read. The system can compute read counts or whether the entire group has read a message by comparing message ids. A middle ground is batching: aggregate multiple read events and write them periodically to reduce write amplification. Each strategy trades write volume, read accuracy, and query complexity. Per-message flags give precise history but are costly. Last-read pointers are compact and efficient for showing "read by N people" or highlighting unread messages, but they lose per-message per-user history. Batching reduces load but increases latency for the sender seeing that their message was read. When designing, consider privacy settings as well—if users can disable read receipts, avoid writing read events for that user. The right solution depends on group sizes, expected read latency, and acceptable storage and write costs.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 11.10 › Read Receipts: Group Strategies
Comparison of approaches
Per-message per-user
Most precise. High write volume for active groups.
Last-read pointer
Compact and efficient. Good for read counts and unread deltas.
Batched updates
Aggregate reads to reduce writes; increases visibility latency.
Design rule: choose the smallest write pattern that satisfies your product need for accuracy and timeliness. For very large groups, prefer last-read pointers or counts instead of full per-message tracking.
Privacy
Respect opt-outs by suppressing read-event writes for users who disable receipts.
Race conditions
Handle concurrent reads across devices by updating last_read to the highest sequence number observed.

screens.title: Integrating presence, typing, and receipts into chat architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating these features involves clear boundaries and event flows between Chat Servers, the Presence Service, Pub/Sub channels, and the Message Database. Chat Servers accept WebSocket connections from clients and are the single place where client events originate. For presence, chat servers update the Presence Service—usually a Redis cluster—when a client connects, disconnects, or on each heartbeat. The Presence Service publishes status change events so other chat servers and interested services can show live status. Typing indicators are emitted by chat servers to Redis Pub/Sub channels keyed by chat_id and are ephemeral; subscribers display them without persistence. Read receipts are reported back to chat servers by clients when messages are viewed; the chat server then updates the Message Database (status field or last_read pointer) and notifies the sender via a push or Pub/Sub. Keep responsibilities separated: presence should not be mixed with message persistence, and typing should remain ephemeral. Microservice separation helps you scale components independently and reason about failure modes. Finally, add monitoring on heartbeat rates, pub/sub throughput, and write rates for receipts so you can detect overloads and tune batching or TTLs as needed.

Typing indicators are emitted by chat servers to Redis Pub/Sub channels keyed by chat_id and are ephemeral; subscribers display them without persistence. Read receipts are reported back to chat servers by clients when messages are viewed; the chat server then updates the Message Database (status field or last_read pointer) and notifies the sender via a push or Pub/Sub. Keep responsibilities separated: presence should not be mixed with message persistence, and typing should remain ephemeral. Microservice separation helps you scale components independently and reason about failure modes. Finally, add monitoring on heartbeat rates, pub/sub throughput, and write rates for receipts so you can detect overloads and tune batching or TTLs as needed.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: When building these features, watch out for a handful of common mistakes that create incorrect UX or system strain. First, over-polling for presence causes unnecessary load; prefer Pub/Sub subscriptions rather than client polling. Second, spamming typing events without debounce floods channels and wastes bandwidth; debounce on the client and send a single typing_start then a typing_stop after idle. Third, inaccurate presence happens when systems rely only on client disconnect events; always use heartbeats to detect abrupt network cuts. Fourth, privacy matters: never enable read receipts by default without an opt-out or clearly documented behavior. Fifth, updating message status for every message for every user in large groups creates massive write amplification; use last_read pointers or batching strategies to reduce writes. Finally, be mindful of race conditions where multiple clients for the same user (phone and desktop) may update read or delivered states concurrently; resolve by choosing last-write-wins on the highest message id or using per-device sequence numbers. Addressing these pitfalls early preserves both user trust and system performance. Common mistakes and safety notes

Over-polling for presence
Use Pub/Sub rather than frequent client polling to avoid unnecessary load.
Spamming typing events
Debounce on the client and limit scope to small groups.
Relying on disconnects alone
Always combine heartbeats with disconnect events to detect abrupt failures.
Privacy violations
Allow users to disable read receipts and enforce that preference server-side.
Write amplification
Avoid per-message per-user writes in large groups; use last_read or batching instead.
Race conditions
Resolve concurrent updates by using message sequence numbers or highest-last-write logic.
Warning

Small UI features can create large system costs—design conservatively and monitor the real traffic patterns.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how presence, typing indicators, and read receipts turn a basic messaging pipeline into a responsive, social experience. Presence tells the system who is available now; typing indicators give real-time micro-feedback that someone intends to send a message; and read receipts close the loop so senders know their message was actually seen. These features are small at the UI level but require careful architecture at scale. We will use Redis for fast presence storage and Pub/Sub for ephemeral events, discuss heartbeats that prevent stale online statuses, and examine how message state moves from sent to delivered to read. You will also see practical trade-offs: how frequent heartbeats affect load, why typing events must be debounced, and how read receipts introduce write amplification and privacy decisions. By the end you should be able to design a dedicated Presence Service, implement typing broadcasts for small conversations, and choose an approach for read receipts that balances accuracy, performance, and user privacy. Consider: when would you accept eventual consistency for read receipts versus needing near-real-time certainty?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design and reason about presence, typing indicators, and read receipts in a production chat system. First, you will design a scalable Presence Service that records online status and last_seen, and uses heartbeats to avoid stale states. Second, you will implement lightweight typing indicators that use debounce and ephemeral Pub/Sub so they don't overwhelm the network. Third, you will understand how message state transitions from sent to delivered to read, how to model status in your message schema, and how to batch or limit updates to reduce write amplification. Finally, you will integrate these features into a chat architecture so presence updates, typing broadcasts, and receipt notifications flow correctly between chat servers, Redis, and the message store. Each objective focuses on practical trade-offs: latency versus consistency, ephemeral data versus persisted state, and privacy controls for receipts.

In this second objectives screen we focus on the concrete techniques and trade-offs that make presence and receipts work in production. You will practice using Redis Hashes or key-value patterns to store user state, and learn how Pub/Sub enables low-latency distribution of ephemeral updates. You will apply heartbeats to detect abrupt client disconnects and design timeouts that balance promptness with false positives. For typing indicators you will adopt client-side debouncing and scope indicators to small groups or direct messages only, keeping public channels quiet. For read receipts you will reason about per-user writes versus batching or tracking only the last-read message, which reduces write amplification in group chats. You will also consider privacy: provide an opt-out for read receipts and ensure your service enforces that preference. Each objective links a concrete implementation pattern to a measurable system trade-off, so you can choose the right approach during design interviews and real systems work.

A Presence Service has three core responsibilities: record when a user connects or disconnects, expose a way to query a user's status, and notify interested parties when statuses change. Practically, that means storing a small record per user—status, last_seen timestamp, and the server_id that hosts the connection. Redis is an excellent fit because it is in-memory, fast, and offers atomic hash operations for these small records. A common key design is presence:user_id mapped to a hash with fields status, last_seen, and server_id. This keeps reads and writes O(1) and keeps the data model simple for other services to consume. The service should expose two access patterns: direct lookups for on-demand queries, and Pub/Sub notifications for real-time subscribers. One important misconception to avoid is believing a single central store is enough for availability; use clustering or sharding to distribute load. Also avoid storing large session blobs in presence records—keep the data minimal to prevent excessive memory pressure. A correct design isolates presence as a small, horizontally scalable microservice that answers the binary but time-sensitive question: is this user online right now?

When you store presence in Redis, pick a compact, consistent key pattern and keep the record tiny. A common pattern is presence:user_id mapped to a Redis hash with fields status, last_seen, and server_id. Status is a short string like online or offline; last_seen is a timestamp used to detect stale heartbeats; server_id indicates which chat server currently hosts that connection. Hashes are ideal because they allow atomic updates to individual fields without replacing the entire value. Avoid storing session-heavy data or long JSON blobs in presence keys. Instead, store only the information needed for other services to decide whether to push a notification or to display an online badge. Also consider TTLs for inactive keys so memory clears for long-away users. Remember a misconception: Redis persistence options exist, but presence usually relies on in-memory semantics and Pub/Sub; don't rely on persistence for presence correctness. Instead, use clustering and replication to handle availability and failover. Storing presence in Redis means use presence:user_id → hset fields status, last_seen, server_id and ttl to evict stale entries.. In practical terms, key patterns: hashes, keys, and what to store. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Heartbeats are periodic keep-alive signals that tell the Presence Service a client is still connected. A typical pattern is for a chat server to send a heartbeat for each connected client every fixed interval, for example every five seconds. The Presence Service updates last_seen when it receives a heartbeat. If last_seen is older than an offline timeout window—commonly 30 to 60 seconds—the Presence Service marks the user offline. This handles abrupt network drops where the server does not receive a formal disconnect. Implementing heartbeats requires careful tuning: a very short interval increases load and network chatter, while a very long interval delays detection of offline clients. Another important point is to avoid relying solely on TCP disconnect events; those are not always delivered promptly. Use heartbeats plus graceful disconnects when possible. A common misconception is that a single missed heartbeat should immediately make a user offline; instead, use a timeout window to avoid flapping for temporary network jitter. In short, heartbeats provide liveness information that the Presence Service uses to keep online state accurate. Heartbeats and timeout detection means send regular heartbeats and mark offline after a timeout window; tune interval versus timeout to balance accuracy and load.. In practical terms, how chat servers keep presence accurate when clients disconnect abruptly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Typing indicators are small ephemeral events that make conversations feel active. The canonical flow is simple: when a user begins typing the client sends a typing_start event to its Chat Server; the server publishes the event to a Pub/Sub channel for that chat_id; other clients subscribed to that chat receive the event and display "User X is typing...". When typing stops—either after a timeout on inactivity or when the message is sent—the client sends typing_stop and the event is broadcast. In practice there are several important best practices. First, debounce typing_start on the client so you don’t publish an event on every keypress. A common pattern is to send typing_start once and then suppress further events for a short window. Second, restrict typing indicators to direct messages or small group chats; in large public channels typing indicators create noise. Third, treat typing events as ephemeral: do not persist them to the message database. Redis Pub/Sub is ideal for this ephemeral broadcast because it keeps the pipeline simple without creating durable writes. Be aware of network load and avoid sending high-frequency typing updates from low-quality connections. Finally, remember that indicators are UI affordances — they do not guarantee a message will be sent.

Read receipts describe stages of a message lifecycle that inform the sender about delivery and consumption. Start with a sent state when the message is persisted to the message store and acknowledged by the sender's client. A delivered state is reached when the message is successfully pushed to the recipient's client and the client acknowledges receipt with an ACK. A read state occurs when the recipient actually views the message, for example when the message is scrolled into view or when the conversation becomes active; the client sends a read event for that message_id or the last message seen. To support these states you need a status field in the messages table, and ideally a mechanism to update that field when ACK or read events arrive. In group chats, tracking per-user read for every message is write-heavy; common strategies are to maintain a last_read pointer per user per conversation or to provide a read-by count. Privacy is important: users should be able to disable read receipts, which changes how and whether the client sends read events. The correct model maps UI expectations to minimal database writes while preserving reasonable accuracy for sender feedback.

Group chats present a scaling problem for read receipts. One approach is to record a read flag for every message and every member, which gives precise per-user per-message visibility but generates a huge number of writes as each user reads messages. An alternative is to maintain a last_read pointer per user per conversation: when a user reads up to message X, update their last_read. The system can compute read counts or whether the entire group has read a message by comparing message ids. A middle ground is batching: aggregate multiple read events and write them periodically to reduce write amplification. Each strategy trades write volume, read accuracy, and query complexity. Per-message flags give precise history but are costly. Last-read pointers are compact and efficient for showing "read by N people" or highlighting unread messages, but they lose per-message per-user history. Batching reduces load but increases latency for the sender seeing that their message was read. When designing, consider privacy settings as well—if users can disable read receipts, avoid writing read events for that user. The right solution depends on group sizes, expected read latency, and acceptable storage and write costs.

Integrating these features involves clear boundaries and event flows between Chat Servers, the Presence Service, Pub/Sub channels, and the Message Database. Chat Servers accept WebSocket connections from clients and are the single place where client events originate. For presence, chat servers update the Presence Service—usually a Redis cluster—when a client connects, disconnects, or on each heartbeat. The Presence Service publishes status change events so other chat servers and interested services can show live status. Typing indicators are emitted by chat servers to Redis Pub/Sub channels keyed by chat_id and are ephemeral; subscribers display them without persistence. Read receipts are reported back to chat servers by clients when messages are viewed; the chat server then updates the Message Database (status field or last_read pointer) and notifies the sender via a push or Pub/Sub. Keep responsibilities separated: presence should not be mixed with message persistence, and typing should remain ephemeral. Microservice separation helps you scale components independently and reason about failure modes. Finally, add monitoring on heartbeat rates, pub/sub throughput, and write rates for receipts so you can detect overloads and tune batching or TTLs as needed.

Look more closely at the simulator functions to see how presence behavior maps to Redis operations. The update_presence function writes a hash using HMSET or HSET with keys status, last_seen, and server_id, and optionally publishes a JSON payload on a presence topic. connect_user registers the user in the server's active_users map and calls update_presence with status online. disconnect_user removes the user from active_users and sets status to offline. The heartbeat thread iterates over active_users at HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS and calls update_presence to refresh last_seen. The helper get_user_status_from_redis reads the presence hash with HGETALL and interprets last_seen numerically; if the recorded last_seen is older than OFFLINE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS it returns a status of offline (timeout). When building these features, watch out for a handful of common mistakes that create incorrect UX or system strain. First, over-polling for presence causes unnecessary load; prefer Pub/Sub subscriptions rather than client polling. Second, spamming typing events without debounce floods channels and wastes bandwidth; debounce on the client and send a single typing_start then a typing_stop after idle. Third, inaccurate presence happens when systems rely only on client disconnect events; always use heartbeats to detect abrupt network cuts. Fourth, privacy matters: never enable read receipts by default without an opt-out or clearly documented behavior. Fifth, updating message status for every message for every user in large groups creates massive write amplification; use last_read pointers or batching strategies to reduce writes. Finally, be mindful of race conditions where multiple clients for the same user (phone and desktop) may update read or delivered states concurrently; resolve by choosing last-write-wins on the highest message id or using per-device sequence numbers. Addressing these pitfalls early preserves both user trust and system performance. These are the core concepts to carry forward. First, a Presence Service is a dedicated component that tracks online/offline state and last_seen. Second, a Heartbeat is a periodic keep-alive used to detect abrupt disconnections and should be tuned with a sensible timeout. Third, Redis Pub/Sub is an efficient mechanism for broadcasting ephemeral status and typing events to interested subscribers. Internalizing these definitions helps you map product requirements to technical patterns: ephemeral updates use Pub/Sub, liveness needs heartbeats, and minimal in-memory records power presence queries. Three more concepts to keep in mind when designing: Typing Indicator is an ephemeral UI signal that should be debounced and scoped to small conversations; Read Receipt is a message lifecycle signal that moves from sent to delivered to read and requires database updates or last-read pointers; Debouncing is a rate-limiting technique that prevents event spam by batching or suppressing repeated signals for a short time. Understanding these patterns helps you make pragmatic choices: limit typing indicators to avoid noise, batch or pointer-based receipts to reduce writes, and debounce frequent UI events to protect network and server resources.
